title: Blessings all day
hookLine: a rabbi of the Talmud taught a hundred blessings a day, scattered through the ordinary hours

cards: A hundred. That's the number Rabbi Meir named. A person, he taught, as the Talmud records, is obliged to say a hundred blessings every day.
Not a hundred long prayers in a service. A hundred short sentences, scattered through the ordinary hours: on waking, before bread, after washing the hands, on hearing thunder.
A hundred sounds like a great deal, until you see how small each one is, and how many things in an ordinary day could be stopped for and noticed.

teach.b: You met the Jewish blessing back on day two hundred fifty; today, a whole day of them. A beracha has a shape people come to recognize.

It opens by speaking to God directly, blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, then names what's in front of the person: the one who brings bread from the earth, the one who creates the fruit of the vine.
The Mishnah gives a whole chapter to blessings for things a person might meet: lightning and thunder, mountains and the sea, good news, and bad news too.
The Talmud records a blessing for after using the bathroom, thanking God for a body made with openings that work as they should. Nothing is too ordinary to be noticed.

teach.h: A SMALL DOOR BEFORE THE THING.
teach.b: A blessing comes before or alongside the thing, so it works like a small door. You don't just eat the apple. You stop, see that there is an apple, name where it came from, and then eat.
The Talmud makes a striking claim: whoever enjoys something of this world without a blessing is like someone who has taken what belongs to heaven.

The verse it leans on is from the Psalms, in the King James: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Read this way, a hundred blessings is less a quota than a way of walking through a day with the doors open.

how: Observant Jews say short blessings throughout the day, on waking, before and after eating, after using the bathroom, and on seeing or hearing things like thunder, the sea or good news, aiming for a hundred a day.

games.q: you're about to bite into an apple. what does the practice of blessings do with this moment?
o: eat now, and give thanks later at a longer prayer.
stop, name where it came from, then eat.
skip it: an apple is too ordinary for a blessing.
games.why: a blessing works like a small door before the thing. you stop, see the apple, name its source, then eat. nothing is too ordinary.

practice: Look around slowly for five things: the chair under you, the air coming in, a sound from outside, your own hands, the light in the room, and stay with each long enough to really see it.
If you pray, you can use the old opening, blessed are you, and name the thing; if you don't, simply say a quiet thank you for it inside. Five small stops.

wordCard.voice: Blessings all day. Short Jewish blessings, scattered through the ordinary hours, a hundred of them in Rabbi Meir's teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a blessing; the plural, berachot, names the Mishnah's tractate on blessings.

carryVoice: Your line: a hundred blessings. By evening, a person has stopped a hundred times to notice something given. See you tomorrow.
